title: BUG: LogisticRegression (and other GLMs) can silently return badly wrong coefficients on off-centered data
body:
> [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact scikit-learn's linear models split into two families with very different handling of un-centered features: - `LinearRegression`, `Ridge`, `Lasso`, `ElasticNet` go through `_preprocess_data`, which centers `X` and `y` (explicitly for dense data, algebraically for sparse) before solving, then reconstructs the intercept afterward. Centering is a pure reparametrization here: for any fixed `coef`, shifting `X` by a constant only shifts the intercept, and the L1/L2 penalty doesn't touch the intercept, so the optimal `coef` is mathematically invariant to any additive shift of the features. Ridge/Lasso exploit this to shield users from poor numerical stability on high mean to variance ratio features. - `LogisticRegression`, `PoissonRegressor`, `GammaRegressor`, `TweedieRegressor` (the `LinearModelLoss` + `NewtonSolver`/lbfgs/newton-cg/newton-cholesky family) do **not** do this. The intercept is just another free parameter solved jointly with the coefficients directly on the raw `X`. There is no `_preprocess_data`-equivalent step. The same invariance holds mathematically for this second family too (same argument: additive shift + unpenalized intercept), but because nothing centers the data first, the solvers can lose that invariance numerically. Concretely: - `newton-cholesky` builds its Hessian from the raw `[X, 1]` design. Eliminating the intercept column during Cholesky factorization implicitly computes `X.T @ X - n * mean(X) * mean(X).T` which can yield catastrophic-cancellation-prone quantity. The scipy solver normally fires a warning or an error in this case, so at least, it's visible for users something is wrong. - `lbfgs` doesn't have a cancellation problem in this sense, but its gradient-norm convergence check can be satisfied prematurely on badly-offset data, silently stopping far from the true optimum, with **no warning at all**. User-facing impact: any real dataset with a feature that's far from zero-mean relative to its variance (a year, a timestamp, an age, a physical measurement with an offset unit) can silently produce badly wrong `coef_`/`intercept_` for these estimators, without any indication something went wrong. I stumbled on this while investigating numerical-stability discussions in #34793 (Ridge's cholesky centering trick). ### Steps/Code to Reproduce Sweep used to generate the plot below:
```python import warnings import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.linear_model import ( LinearRegression, LogisticRegression, Ridge, TweedieRegressor, PoissonRegressor, ElasticNet, ) def relative_error_vs_mean_variance_ratio( linear_estimator, dtype="float32", random_seed=0, max_ratio=1e5 ): rng = np.random.RandomState(random_seed) n_samples, n_features = 5000, 5 X = rng.normal(size=(n_samples, n_features)) true_coef = rng.normal(size=n_features) proba = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X @ true_coef))) y = (rng.uniform(size=n_samples) < proba).astype(int) X, y = X.astype(dtype), y.astype(dtype) linear_estimator.fit(X, y) ref = linear_estimator.coef_.copy() assert np.linalg.norm(ref) > 0.1 # we want coefs that aren't too small ratios = np.logspace(0, np.log10(max_ratio), num=30) errors, has_warnings = [], [] for offset in ratios: with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught: linear_estimator.fit((X + offset).astype(dtype), y) shifted = linear_estimator.coef_.copy() errors.append(np.linalg.norm(shifted - ref) / np.linalg.norm(ref)) has_warnings.append(bool(caught)) return ratios, np.array(errors), np.array(has_warnings) models = [ Ridge(solver="cholesky", alpha=1 / 5000), Ridge(solver="lbfgs", positive=True, alpha=1 / 5000), ElasticNet(alpha=1 / 5000), LinearRegression(), # GLMs: LogisticRegression(solver="lbfgs"), LogisticRegression(solver="newton-cholesky"), TweedieRegressor(solver="lbfgs", alpha=1 / 5000), TweedieRegressor(solver="newton-cholesky", alpha=1 / 5000), PoissonRegressor(solver="lbfgs", alpha=1 / 5000), PoissonRegressor(solver="newton-cholesky", alpha=1 / 5000), ] dtypes = ["float32", "float64"] n_cols = 2 n_rows = -(-len(models) // n_cols) # ceil division fig, axes = plt.subplots( n_rows, n_cols, figsize=(5 * n_cols, 3 * n_rows), sharex=True, sharey=True ) axes = axes.ravel() for ax, model in zip(axes, models): results = [relative_error_vs_mean_variance_ratio(model, dtype=dtype) for dtype in dtypes] for (ratios, errors, has_warnings), dtype in zip(results, dtypes): line, = ax.plot(ratios, errors, label=dtype) ax.scatter( ratios[has_warnings], errors[has_warnings], marker="x", s=10, color=line.get_color(), ) ax.set_ylim(0, 1.02) ax.set_xscale("log") ax.set_title(str(model), fontsize=9) ax.tick_params(axis="x", which="both", labelbottom=True) ax.set_xlabel("mean/variance ratio") for ax in axes[len(models):]: ax.axis("off") for ax in axes[::n_cols]: ax.set_ylabel("relative error") axes[0].legend() fig.tight_layout() ```
### Expected Results Fitting on `X + offset` should not change `coef_` (more than floating point noise) or at the very least should not change `coef_` without a warning. ### Actual Results The grid below (generated by the reproducer snippet) sweeps the feature mean/variance ratio (`X + ratio`, unit-variance `X`) from 1 to 1e5, one subplot per estimator, and plots the relative error of `coef_` against the ratio=0 reference, for both `float32` and `float64`, with `×` marking points where a warning was raised: - `Ridge`, `LinearRegression`, `ElasticNet` (top two rows, the `_preprocess_data` family): error stays ~0 across the entire range, in both dtypes. A blip only appears in float32 at the extreme end (ratio ≥1e4), never in float64. - `LogisticRegression`, `TweedieRegressor`, `PoissonRegressor` (bottom three rows, the GLM family), with *either* solver (lbfgs or newton-cholesky): garbage coefficients starting at a ratio as low as ~20-100 in float32 and ~300-5000 in float64. ### Versions ```shell System: python: 3.14.6 (main, Jun 23 2026, 15:18:23) [Clang 22.1.3 ] executable: /home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/bin/python machine: Linux-6.17.0-1032-oem-x86_64-with-glibc2.39 Python dependencies: sklearn: 1.10.dev0 pip: None setuptools: None numpy: 2.5.3 scipy: 1.18.1 Cython: 3.3.0 pandas: 3.0.5 matplotlib: 3.11.1 joblib: 1.6.0 threadpoolctl: 3.6.0 narwhals: 2.26.0 Built with OpenMP: True threadpoolctl info: user_api: blas internal_api: openblas num_threads: 14 prefix: libscipy_openblas filepath: /home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/lib/python3.14/site-packages/numpy.libs/libscipy_openblas64_-f48b354e.so version: 0.3.34.106.0 threading_layer: pthreads architecture: Haswell user_api: blas internal_api: openblas num_threads: 14 prefix: libscipy_openblas filepath: /home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/lib/python3.14/site-packages/scipy.libs/libscipy_openblas-5f890258.so version: 0.3.31.dev threading_layer: pthreads architecture: Haswell user_api: openmp internal_api: openmp num_threads: 14 prefix: libgomp filepath: /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libgomp.so.1.0.0 version: None ``` ### Interest in fixing the bug Yes. I'm about to open a PR with a proposed fixed: detecting high mean/variance ratio and explicitly recentering if needed.

title: BUG: Explicit validation data does not enable HistGradientBoosting automatic early stopping

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue requires triage

body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`HistGradientBoostingRegressor` and `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` accept explicit `X_val` and `y_val` but do not enable early stopping with `early_stopping="auto"` on a small training set. This also affects calls that leave `early_stopping` at its default value, `"auto"`.

In the example below, both estimators fit successfully on 30 training samples, but `do_early_stopping_` is `False` and `validation_score_` is empty. Changing only `early_stopping` to `True` enables monitoring of the same validation data and records four validation scores.

The user-facing problem is that the supplied validation data does not participate in the early-stopping checks, despite the documented automatic activation. This is not just missing score history: the validation-based stopping criterion is disabled. In longer runs, this could cause unnecessary boosting iterations and potentially affect generalization. The example establishes disabled monitoring and stopping checks; it does not establish degraded predictions or a production incident.

A workaround is to set `early_stopping=True` explicitly when providing validation arrays.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import sklearn
from sklearn.ensemble import (
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
    HistGradientBoostingRegressor,
)

print(sklearn.__version__)
X = np.arange(40.0).reshape(-1, 1)

for estimator_class in (
    HistGradientBoostingRegressor,
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
):
    y = (
        np.sin(X[:, 0])
        if estimator_class is HistGradientBoostingRegressor
        else np.arange(40) % 2
    )
    for mode in ("auto", True):
        estimator = estimator_class(
            early_stopping=mode, max_iter=3, random_state=0
        ).fit(X[:30], y[:30], X_val=X[30:], y_val=y[30:])
        print(
            estimator_class.__name__, mode,
            estimator.do_early_stopping_,
            len(estimator.validation_score_),
        )
```

### Expected Results

With explicit validation arrays, both modes should enable early stopping for both estimators, even with only 30 training samples:

```text
1.9.0
HistGradientBoostingRegressor auto True 4
HistGradientBoostingRegressor True True 4
HistGradientBoostingClassifier auto True 4
HistGradientBoostingClassifier True True 4
```

The version 1.9 documentation specifies automatic activation when either the training sample count exceeds 10,000 or `X_val` and `y_val` are supplied to `fit`:

- [HistGradientBoostingRegressor documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/1.9/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor.html)
- [HistGradientBoostingClassifier documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/1.9/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingClassifier.html)

Four scores correspond to the initial model plus three completed boosting iterations. The example tests whether validation monitoring is enabled, not whether fitting must terminate before `max_iter`.

### Actual Results

The reported run on scikit-learn 1.9.0 produced:

```text
1.9.0
HistGradientBoostingRegressor auto False 0
HistGradientBoostingRegressor True True 4
HistGradientBoostingClassifier auto False 0
HistGradientBoostingClassifier True True 4
```

No exception is raised. Automatic mode leaves early stopping disabled and records no validation scores, while explicit `True` monitors the same validation data.

### Versions

```shell
1.9.0
1.9.1
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

In [`BaseHistGradientBoosting.fit` at tag 1.9.0](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.0/sklearn/ensemble/_hist_gradient_boosting/gradient_boosting.py), the automatic-mode decision only checks the training sample count:

```python
if self.early_stopping == "auto":
    self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000
```

The method has already calculated `validation_data_provided` and checked that both validation arrays are supplied together, but that flag is not included in the automatic-mode decision.

A candidate fix is:

```diff
- self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000
+ self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000 or validation_data_provided
```

This is a source-based suggestion, not a tested patch.

A regression test should cover both estimator classes with a small training set, explicit validation arrays, and `early_stopping="auto"`, and check:

```python
assert estimator.do_early_stopping_
assert len(estimator.validation_score_) == estimator.n_iter_ + 1
```

Keep `early_stopping=True` as a passing control. Additional coverage should preserve the sample-count rule when validation arrays are absent, including the 10,000-sample boundary, and preserve the existing validation-argument errors.

Related work: [#18748](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/18748) requested custom validation-set support, and [#27124](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/27124) introduced the explicit validation arguments. These references do not establish that no duplicate report exists.

body:
Fixes #35032.

### Summary
This PR fixes a bug where `HistGradientBoostingRegressor` and `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` do not enable early stopping with `early_stopping="auto"` on a small training set, even when validation data (`X_val`, `y_val`) is explicitly provided.

### Root Cause
In `_hist_gradient_boosting/gradient_boosting.py`, the `auto` mode check only considered if `n_samples > 10_000`, ignoring the explicitly provided validation data:
```python
        if self.early_stopping == "auto":
            self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000
```

### Changes
* Modified the automatic activation logic to also check `validation_data_provided`:
  ```python
          if self.early_stopping == "auto":
              self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000 or validation_data_provided
  ```
* Added a non-regression test `test_early_stopping_auto_with_validation_data` in `test_gradient_boosting.py`.

### Testing
Added a regression test to verify that `early_stopping="auto"` activates early stopping behavior and tracks validation scores properly when `X_val` and `y_val` are supplied for both `HistGradientBoostingRegressor` and `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` with <10,000 samples.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

The [`RFECV` API reference](https://scikit-learn.org/1.9/modules/generated/sklearn.feature_selection.RFECV.html) documents both `cv_results_["split(k)_ranking"]` and `cv_results_["split(k)_support"]` as arrays with shape `(n_subsets_of_features,)`.

Both arrays actually have shape `(n_subsets_of_features, n_features)`, where `n_features` is the number of original input features, `X.shape[1]`. Each row contains a rank or a selection indicator for every original feature. In contrast, `split(k)_test_score` has one scalar per evaluated subset and correctly has shape `(n_subsets_of_features,)`.

### User-facing impact

The documented shape can mislead users interpreting per-fold rankings or selection masks, for example when examining feature-selection stability. Indexing a ranking/support result by subset returns a vector over original features, not a scalar. Code written around the documented one-dimensional structure could therefore use the wrong indexing or aggregation.

This is a documentation mismatch. The reproducer does not show incorrect feature selection, scores, or predictions, and no change to the returned arrays is requested.

### Minimal reproducer

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_selection import RFECV
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

X = np.column_stack(
    (np.arange(10.), np.tile([0., 1.], 5), np.ones(10))
)
selector = RFECV(
    Ridge(), cv=2, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error"
).fit(X, np.arange(10.))

for key in ("split0_ranking", "split0_support", "split0_test_score"):
    print(key, selector.cv_results_[key].shape)

assert selector.cv_results_["split0_ranking"].shape == (3, 3)
assert selector.cv_results_["split0_support"].shape == (3, 3)
assert selector.cv_results_["split0_test_score"].shape == (3,)
```

### Observed shapes

```text
split0_ranking (3, 3)
split0_support (3, 3)
split0_test_score (3,)
```

The assertions pass. There are three evaluated subset sizes and three original features.

### Verification scope

Runtime observation: scikit-learn 1.9.0, NumPy 2.5.2, and Python 3.14.7.

The affected `/1.9/` documentation page was inspected on September 11, 2026 and was labelled 1.9.1. The documentation version and tested runtime version are distinct: the 1.9.1 runtime was not tested for this report.

The [1.9.0 implementation](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.0/sklearn/feature_selection/_rfe.py) also explains the feature axis: it collects rankings and supports over folds, evaluated subsets, and original features, then indexes out the fold axis when assigning each per-split result.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Update the two shape annotations in the `RFECV` class docstring in [`sklearn/feature_selection/_rfe.py`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.0/sklearn/feature_selection/_rfe.py):

```diff
-        split(k)_ranking : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features,)
+        split(k)_ranking : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features, n_features)

-        split(k)_support : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features,)
+        split(k)_support : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features, n_features)
```

Please also clarify the axis meanings in the descriptions:

- Rows correspond to the evaluated subset sizes, ordered consistently with `cv_results_["n_features"]`.
- Columns correspond to the original input features, in their original order. This axis does not shrink as features are eliminated and is not the final selected-feature count, `n_features_`.

For example, `cv_results_["split0_support"][i, j]` indicates whether original feature `j` was selected for the subset represented by row `i` in split 0.

The Notes paragraph also describes the "size" of every `cv_results_` array using the subset-count formula. Consider calling this the **length of the first axis** instead, since the ranking and support arrays are two-dimensional.

This request concerns the docstring and generated API reference only; the existing two-dimensional outputs should remain unchanged.

title: BUG: Pipeline.fit_predict skips transform_input for final-step metadata

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue requires triage

body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

With metadata routing enabled and `transform_input=["X_val"]`, `Pipeline.fit_predict` passes transformed training data to the final estimator but leaves `X_val` untransformed. An otherwise identical call to `Pipeline.fit` transforms `X_val` correctly.

In the reproducer, the final estimator receives `X_val = [[15.0]]` through `fit_predict`, although the fitted scaler maps that value to `[[0.0]]`. No exception is raised.

This can put training data and validation metadata in different feature spaces. An estimator that uses the metadata could therefore compute incorrect validation quantities or make different fitting decisions. Preprocessing that changes the feature count could instead cause a shape error. These are potential consequences; the reproducer demonstrates the incorrect metadata, not a production failure or incorrect predictions from a built-in estimator.

The [documented purpose of `transform_input`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline.html) is to transform selected metadata before the consuming step receives it, including validation data.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import sklearn
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

sklearn.set_config(enable_metadata_routing=True)


class RecordsXVal(RegressorMixin, BaseEstimator):
    def fit(self, X, y, X_val=None):
        self.X_val_seen_ = X_val
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        return np.zeros(len(X))

    def fit_predict(self, X, y, X_val=None):
        return self.fit(X, y, X_val=X_val).predict(X)


X = np.array([[0.0], [10.0], [20.0], [30.0]])
y = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
X_val = np.array([[15.0]])

for method in ("fit", "fit_predict"):
    pipe = Pipeline(
        [
            ("scale", StandardScaler()),
            ("model", RecordsXVal().set_fit_request(X_val=True)),
        ],
        transform_input=["X_val"],
    )
    getattr(pipe, method)(X, y, X_val=X_val)
    print(
        sklearn.__version__,
        method,
        "final step received X_val =",
        pipe[-1].X_val_seen_.ravel(),
    )
```

### Expected Results

Both methods should pass the transformed validation value to the final estimator:

```text
1.9.1 fit final step received X_val = [0.]
1.9.1 fit_predict final step received X_val = [0.]
```

The same is expected on 1.9.0. The scaler is fitted on `[0, 10, 20, 30]`, whose mean is `15`, so transforming `[[15.0]]` gives `[[0.0]]`.

### Actual Results

Running the reproducer separately in the two affected environments produced:

```text
1.9.1 fit final step received X_val = [0.]
1.9.1 fit_predict final step received X_val = [15.]
1.9.0 fit final step received X_val = [0.]
1.9.0 fit_predict final step received X_val = [15.]
```

No exception is raised. Only `fit_predict` passes the original validation value to the final estimator.

### Versions

```shell
1.9.0
1.9.1
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

The likely cause is the final-step parameter handling in [`Pipeline.fit_predict`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.1/sklearn/pipeline.py):

```python
params_last_step = routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]]
```

Unlike `fit` and `fit_transform`, this does not use `_get_metadata_for_step` for the final estimator. The intermediate-step fix in [#34201](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34201/files) does not change that final-step assignment.

A candidate fix is:

```diff
- params_last_step = routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]]
+ params_last_step = self._get_metadata_for_step(
+     step_idx=len(self) - 1,
+     step_params=routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]],
+     all_params=params,
+ )
```

A regression test should assert that the final estimator receives `pipe[:-1].transform(X_val)` after `fit_predict`, with `fit` as a passing control. For example, append this assertion after the reproducer's loop:

```python
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    pipe[-1].X_val_seen_,
    pipe[:-1].transform(X_val),
)
```

This suggestion still needs validation against a patched target-version checkout and the relevant upstream tests.

body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs
Part 8 of #33160, follow-up of #34561.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
#34561 introduced the `solver="newton-cd"` which uses coordinate descent without gram matrix (=Hessian), i.e. like `ElasticNet(precompute=False).` It only uses the full hessian implicitly. This works by **taking the square root** of the Hessian (X'WX) and formulating the update step (one Newton iteration) as a least squares problem with penalty.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> This does not work out of the box for the multinomial/multiclass setting because the pointwise hessian (W) is not diagonal.
> Several attempts of approximations that e.g. glmnet uses don't converge on simple problems.

This PR extends #34561 by introducing a dedicated coordinate descent solver for the multinomial. It uses an analytic LDL decomposition of the pointwise hessian (aka covariance of the multinomial) in order to take the square root of X'WX.

This is a very good solver for `n_features > n_samples`, thus closing this gap in solver options (currently only saga, but it often has concergence issues).

title: TST Add common tests for callback support
body:
This PR is a first batch of common tests for callback support in estimators. So these are common tests for estimators. Common tests for callbacks will come in a different PR.

Here are the first checks that I thought about. We can of course add more check in subsequent PRs when they come to mind.
- add checks in estimator_checks
    - check that an estimator has a single root context
    - check that setup and teardown are called exactly once each
    - check that for each context, on_fit_task_begin and on_fit_task_end are called exactly once and in that order
    - check that the estimator passed to the callback is the one being fitted (particularly useful for meta-estimators)

Since we're using testing helpers outside of the callback module I was not satisfy to import stuff from `sklearn.callback.tests.xxx`, so I moved `callback.tests._common` into `callback._testing` so that we don't import stuff across test files. This is the reason why the diff impacts that many files, but the real stuff happens in `estimator_checks` and `test_common`.

As we usually do for common tests about things that are not part of the scikit-learn compatibility contract, i.e. third-party don't have to use it, I did not include the new checks into `yield_all_checks` but run them in a dedicated common test instead.

I added a list of all the estimator that don't support callbacks yet to skip the test. We'll remove them from the list one at a time when we start adding callback support in more estimators (i.e. after we have merged the metadata routing PR).

title: PRF Mitigation heuristics for HGB scalability
body:
Finally, I have something that has a uniformly positive impact on the 8 scenarios I'm testing:
- Big machine with default OMP settings
- Big machine with `OMP_PROC_BIND=close` (avoids penalizing runs that use fewer threads than what's available on the machine)
- Laptop with active wait disabled (the default behavior of conda-forge packages)
- Laptop with active wait enabled

(× libgomp & libomp for each of those)

And it can be very/hugely beneficial in some scenarios (2-10x speed-ups):
- small to medium datasets on a big machine
- small to medium-big datasets on laptops with active wait disabled

#### Reference Issues/PRs

Implements item 4 (partially), item 5 and item 6 of https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34764#issuecomment-5343004000

I'd also say it closes #14306, though that issue does have some ideas that aren't implemented here, in particular parallelizing over blocks of samples × features when building histograms. Benchmarks show HGB does keep scaling up to 16-32 threads for many medium/big datasets, as long as active wait is enabled, which I'd personally consider good enough for now.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

- Detect whether the OpenMP runtime uses active wait, i.e. whether idle threads spin instead of sleeping while waiting for work (`_openmp_uses_active_wait` in `sklearn/utils/_openmp_helpers.pyx`). This is done by parsing the environment dump the runtime prints under `OMP_DISPLAY_ENV=VERBOSE`, in a short-lived subprocess. Active wait makes rejoining a parallel region much cheaper, so all the heuristics below branch on it.
- Cap the number of threads used to grow each tree, based on the number of features and samples (`BaseHistGradientBoosting._get_heurirstic_optimal_n_threads`), instead of always using every available thread.
- Same idea for binning: `_BinMapper`'s `n_threads` parameter is renamed to `max_n_threads` since it's now only an upper bound, the actual thread count used being derived from the amount of data to bin.
- In `Splitter.split_indices`, fall back to a single-threaded partitioning pass when there isn't enough work per thread to justify the chunking/offset bookkeeping of the multi-threaded version.
- In `Splitter.find_node_split`, when active wait is disabled, skip parallelizing over features when there are too few of them relative to `n_threads`.

#### AI usage disclosure

Mostly not, except for the active wait detection: Claude helped find a way to make the subprocess-based `_openmp_uses_active_wait` fast enough not to matter (result cached after the first call, subprocess kept minimal to avoid a full `import sklearn`).

#### Benchmarks

https://pr-81.sklbench-dashboard-preview.pages.dev/

### Reference Issues/PRs
Closes #28711.
Related to #11865.

**Update June 2026** (scikit-learn sprint)

### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
This PR
- for class `LogisticRegression`
  - deprecates parameter `C` in 1.10
    - will raise warning in 1.12
    - will remove `C` in 1.14
  - introduces the new penalty parameter `alpha`
  - sets default `alpha="1/n_samples" such that it is the same as `C=1`
- for class `LogisticRegressionCV`
  - deprecates the parameter `Cs` 
  - introduces the new penalty parameter `alphas`
  - deprecates attributes `C_` and `Cs_` in 1.10, removal in 1.14 
  - introduces new attributes `alpha_` and `alphas_`

<details>

**NOTE**: This "details" contains the outdate/old content.

**Update March 2026** after merge of #32659.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
This PR
- for class `LogisticRegression`
  - deprecates parameter `C` 
  - introduces the new penalty parameter `alpha`
  - ~~deprecates the parameter `penalty`~~
  - ~~changes the default of `l1_ratio` from `None` to `0`~~
- for class `LogisticRegressionCV`
  - deprecates the parameter `Cs` 
  - introduces the new penalty parameter `alphas`
  - deprecates attributes `C_` and `Cs_`
  - introduces new attributes `alpha_` and `alphas_`
  - ~~deprecates parameter `penalty`~~
  - ~~changes the default of `l1_ratios` from `None` to `(0,)`~~
- for class `StackingClassifier`
  - Additional informative warning for default `final_estimator=None` which uses `LogisticRegression()`
 
</details>

**Note:** Together with #32659, the way to specify penalties is then 100% aligned with 
- `SGDClassifier(alpha=.., loss="log_loss")` (this is even the identical model!)
- `ElasticNet(alpha=.., l1_ratio=..)`
- `Lasso(alpha=)`
- `PoissonRegressor(alpha=)`
- other GLMs

All use `1/(2n) * sum(deviance loss) + alpha/2 * ||w||_2`. See #15657 for further reasons of this choice.

For historians, the parameter `scale_C` which devided `C` by `n_samples` was once deprecated in #821.

<details>

**NOTE:** This is outdated content.

#### Open questions
1. Default `alpha`
   While the future default is currently `alpha=1`, a much smaller value might be better in practice, e.g. alpha=1e-4. Tiny regularization is also the main effect of `C=1` as it scales the penalty by 1/n_samples.

   For optimal prediction $p=P(Y|X)$, the expected log loss is the Shannon entropy (up to a factor) $E[log loss] = H(p) = -p \log(p) - (1-p)\log(1-p)$. The maximum is achieved at p=0.5 with H=0.69, some more values: H(1e-3) = 0.007, H(1e-6) = 1.5e-5. This shows, that `alpha=1` is a pretty strong penalty (for features of scale 1 or smaller).

2. Depending on the default of `alpha`, a good default for `StackingClassifier(final_estimator=..)` is basically no or tiny regularization.

</details>

### Any other comments?
This will be a highly controversial issue, therefore a lot of fun ahead 🎉 

<details>

**Outdated content**
**The main reason for this change is that the current API is objectively bad design.** ~~Currently, I need to specify 3 parameters (`penalty`, `C`, `l1_ratio`) for just 2 effective parameters (the L1 and L2 penalization). On top, it warns a lot when mixing those, e.g. `penalty="l2"` and `l1_ratio=0`, but why on earth...~~

</details>

#### More arguments for `alpha` instead of `C`
1. API consistency: LogisticRegression is the only linear model using an anti-penalty `C`, all the others use penalty `alpha`, see https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/28711#issuecomment-2030156413.
4. Literature:
  - The invention of using a Ridge penalty with logistic regression, https://www.jstor.org/stable/2347628 (Cessie et al 1992), uses a penalty (like `alpha`) and not an anti-penalty (like `C`). The papers for Lasso & Elastic-Net in combination with logreg do the same (use penalty like `alpha`).
  - I have a hard time (=I did not succeed) to find any (famous) ML book like ESL using the anti-penalty.
5. Other reference packages: The most famous R package glmnet (and others) uses a penalty (like `alpha`, they call it `lambda`, but that does not work in Python) and not an anti-penalty (like `C`).
6. Point of view of optimization: the penalty (like `alpha`) version can be seen as regularization to prevent singular behaviour (analogous to Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm), see Nocedal.
7. Original decision and discussion: I cannot find any discussion about the original introduction of `C` vs. `alpha` in LogisticRegression in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/commit/2993becc3dde6c15b11e0f79a05dc8bc022fd9cb. My guess is that liblinear's parameter names were just inherited.
8. Practicality: One never needs `C=0` (`alpha=np.inf`), but `C=np.inf` (`alpha=0`) is used very often. Zero is a much better defined value than infinity.
9. `C` interferes with class weights. Higher class weights means less regularization.
10. The main reason for `C` (and IFAIC its origin) is the analogy with support vector machines. SVM were once very powerful, but have become less and less important in practice. My prediction: this trend will continue.

#### Study of possible default values for the penalty
See https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/32042#issuecomment-4366344257 and the linked notebook https://github.com/lorentzenchr/notebooks/blob/master/logistic_regression_optimal_penalty.ipynb.

#### Reference Issues/PRs

Alternative to #34793: includes its centering trick for Ridge cholesky, but guarded by an a priori check (as suggested in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34793#issuecomment-5810816957).

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

- Ridge cholesky: centering trick from #34793 (the Gram matrix is corrected algebraically instead of materializing a centered copy of X), but only when the mean/variance ratio of the features makes it numerically safe. Otherwise, fall back to explicit centering as in main.

title: Fix normalized BayesianRidge scores_ (#13852)
body:
Fixes #13852.

### Why

`BayesianRidge.scores_` includes the Gaussian likelihood constant but omits the normalization of its two Gamma priors. This makes the reported values incomplete, particularly when comparing different prior hyperparameters. The final score also needs to use the final fitted coefficients.

### Derivation

With `A = lambda I + alpha X.T X` and `mu = alpha A^{-1} X.T y`, completing the square and integrating out the coefficients gives

```
log p(y | X, alpha, lambda)
= 1/2 [p log(lambda) + n log(alpha) - log|A|
       - alpha ||y - X mu||^2 - lambda ||mu||^2 - n log(2 pi)].
```

The existing precision update equations correspond to Gamma priors with shape `alpha_1 + 1` and `lambda_1 + 1` and rates `alpha_2` and `lambda_2`. Thus each prior term `a log(t) - b t` also requires the constant `(a + 1) log(b) - log Gamma(a + 1)` when `b > 0`. At `b = 0`, the prior is improper, so the undefined constant remains omitted. The user guide gives the completed-square derivation, its equivalent covariance-space form, the derivatives, and the fixed-point updates.

### Changes

- Add the two Gamma normalization constants to `scores_` without changing the fitting updates or predictions.
- Evaluate the final score with the final fitted coefficients.
- Clarify the score API, private method name, and normalization caveats for fitted intercepts and sample weights.
- Compare initial and final scores against independent SciPy Gaussian and Gamma log densities for both `n > p` and `p > n`, including zero-rate priors.

### Verification

The 25 BayesianRidge-relevant tests in `sklearn/linear_model/tests/test_bayes.py` pass with the modified source module loaded against the installed scikit-learn 1.8 runtime. This source checkout lacks compiled extensions, so its native test invocation was unavailable. Ruff format and selected lint checks pass.

title: permutation_importance computes non-zero importance for features the model never uses when max_samples < 1

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I'm an undergraduate economics student at UC Davis. I use scikit-learn for data analysis and use permutation importance to understand which features matter. This is my first issue filed against scikit-learn.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

**What:** When `max_samples` is set below 1, features that the model never uses still get non-zero permutation importances. By definition, shuffling a column the model does not look at cannot change the predictions, so its importance should be exactly 0. With `max_samples=1.0` the importance is indeed 0; the problem only appears when a subsample is used.

**My example:** The model only uses feature 0; features 1 and 2 are pure noise that the model never reads. With `max_samples=0.5`, both features 1 and 2 get an importance of −0.0104. The 5 repetitions (`n_repeats=5`) return exactly the same value, so the standard deviation is 0. The bias changes in magnitude and sign with the subsample size: −0.026 at 0.2 and +0.006 at 0.1. This shows it is sampling noise, not a real feature contribution.

**Cause** (I read `sklearn/inspection/_permutation_importance.py`): The baseline score is computed on all rows, while the shuffled score is computed on the subsampled rows only, and the two are subtracted. The difference therefore mixes in the gap between the full-data score and the subsample score, which has nothing to do with the feature. The docstring says a fresh sample is drawn for each repetition; in practice the subsample is drawn once per feature before the repetitions, and all features share the same random seed — so repeating does not average the bias away (std = 0), and every irrelevant feature gets the same bias.

**Impact on users:** `max_samples` exists to save time on large datasets. With this bug, irrelevant features get spuriously positive or negative importances, which can make them look useful or harmful, and can also corrupt feature ranking.

**AI usage disclosure:** I used an AI assistant to help identify this problem and write the reproduction script. The description above is my own, and the reproduction was run on my own computer.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np, sklearn
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score
print(sklearn.__version__)
rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
n = 200
X = rng.randn(n, 3)
y = 3 * X[:, 0] + rng.randn(n)          # only feature 0 matters
X[:, 1:] = rng.randn(n, 2)                # features 1, 2: pure noise
model = LinearRegression().fit(X[:, :1], y)  # model uses ONLY feature 0 ...
class OnlyFirst:                              # ... wrapped so it accepts 3 columns
    def fit(self, X, y): return self
    def predict(self, X): return model.predict(X[:, :1])
    def score(self, X, y): return r2_score(y, self.predict(X))
est = OnlyFirst()

r = permutation_importance(est, X, y, n_repeats=5, max_samples=0.5, random_state=0)
print("importances_mean (max_samples=0.5):", r.importances_mean)
print("importances (features 1,2 are ignored by the model, so must be exactly 0):")
print(r.importances[1:])

# Independent expectation: permuting a column the model never reads cannot change
# predictions, so the permuted score equals the score on the SAME rows -> importance 0.
r_full = permutation_importance(est, X, y, n_repeats=5, max_samples=1.0, random_state=0)
print("importances_mean (max_samples=1.0):", r_full.importances_mean)
print("baseline (all rows) r2:", r2_score(y, est.predict(X)))
for ms in (0.2, 0.1):
    r = permutation_importance(est, X, y, n_repeats=5, max_samples=ms, random_state=0)
    print(f"max_samples={ms}: importances_mean =", r.importances_mean, " importances_std =", r.importances_std)
```

### Expected Results

For every repetition, the importances of features 1 and 2 should be exactly 0 — identical to the result with `max_samples=1.0`.

### Actual Results

#### Reference Issues/PRs

Refs #14228. The new wording is modeled on the RandomForest `n_jobs` docstring from #14628.


#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

This PR only changes the `n_jobs` description in `BaggingClassifier` and `BaggingRegressor`.

The current text says jobs run in parallel "for both fit and predict". That doesn't tell the reader what gets split across the jobs, and for the classifier it misses `predict_proba`, `predict_log_proba` and `decision_function`, which also run in parallel.

The new text names every parallel method and says the work is parallelized by splitting the base estimators across jobs. RandomForest says "over the trees", but Bagging hands each job a group of estimators, so I went with "splitting the base estimators across jobs". `_partition_estimators` makes `min(n_jobs, n_estimators)` groups, which means an `n_jobs` larger than `n_estimators` gives no extra speed-up. The sentences about `None`, `-1` and the Glossary are unchanged.

    python bagging_n_jobs_timing.py --calibrate
    python bagging_n_jobs_timing.py --clf-samples 2500 --reg-samples 3000 \
        --predict-samples 60000 --svc-test 1000 --knn-samples 7500
"""

import argparse
import contextlib
import io
import os
import statistics
import time
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

import joblib

import sklearn
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification, make_regression
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingClassifier, BaggingRegressor
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier, KNeighborsRegressor
from sklearn.svm import SVC

N_JOBS = [1, 2, 4, 6]  # 6 = physical core count of the test machine
N_REPEATS = 5
N_ESTIMATORS = 100
N_FEATURES = 20
RANDOM_STATE = 0
RESULTS_FILE = Path(__file__).with_name("bagging_n_jobs_results.md")

# Thresholds for the pass/FAIL checks
CLEARLY_FASTER = 0.8  # at 2 jobs, a method must take under 80% of its 1-job time
NOISE = 1.1  # a higher n_jobs may be at most 10% slower than the previous one
OOB_FLAT = 0.7  # KNN fit (mostly OOB scoring) must stay above 70% of its 1-job time
CAP_FLAT = 0.9  # with 2 estimators, 4 and 6 jobs must stay above 90% of 2 jobs


def parse_args():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.splitlines()[0])
    parser.add_argument("--calibrate", action="store_true",
                        help="time each step once at n_jobs=1 to size the data")
    parser.add_argument("--clf-samples", type=int, default=8_000,
                        help="training samples for BaggingClassifier")
    parser.add_argument("--reg-samples", type=int, default=8_000,
                        help="training samples for BaggingRegressor")
    parser.add_argument("--predict-samples", type=int, default=50_000,
                        help="samples passed to the prediction methods")
    parser.add_argument("--svc-train", type=int, default=2_000,
                        help="training samples for the SVC decision_function run")
    parser.add_argument("--svc-test", type=int, default=5_000,
                        help="samples passed to decision_function")
    parser.add_argument("--knn-samples", type=int, default=6_000,
                        help="training samples for the KNN OOB control")
    return parser.parse_args()


def make_data(args):
    """Synthetic data, split into a training part and a prediction part."""
    Xc, yc = make_classification(
        n_samples=args.clf_samples + args.predict_samples, n_features=N_FEATURES,
        n_informative=10, random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    )
    Xr, yr = make_regression(
        n_samples=args.reg_samples + args.predict_samples, n_features=N_FEATURES,
        n_informative=10, noise=10.0, random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    )
    Xs, ys = make_classification(
        n_samples=args.svc_train + args.svc_test, n_features=N_FEATURES,
        n_informative=10, random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    )
    Xkc, ykc = make_classification(
        n_samples=args.knn_samples, n_features=N_FEATURES, n_informative=10,
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    )
    Xkr, ykr = make_regression(
        n_samples=args.knn_samples, n_features=N_FEATURES, n_informative=10,
        noise=10.0, random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    )
    n, m, s = args.clf_samples, args.reg_samples, args.svc_train
    return {
        "clf": (Xc[:n], yc[:n], Xc[n:]),
        "reg": (Xr[:m], yr[:m], Xr[m:]),
        "svc": (Xs[:s], ys[:s], Xs[s:]),
        "knn_clf": (Xkc, ykc),
        "knn_reg": (Xkr, ykr),
    }


def run_once(func):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    func()
    return time.perf_counter() - start


def median_time(func):
    """Median wall-clock time of func() over N_REPEATS runs, after one warm-up."""
    func()  # warm-up: starts the worker processes; not recorded
    return statistics.median(run_once(func) for _ in range(N_REPEATS))


def time_fit(label, estimator_class, X, y, **params):
    """Time fit on a fresh estimator for each n_jobs value."""
    print(f"timing {label} ...", flush=True)
    times = {}
    for n in N_JOBS:
        estimator = estimator_class(n_jobs=n, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, **params)
        times[n] = median_time(lambda: estimator.fit(X, y))
    return times


def time_method(label, fitted, method, X):
    """Time one prediction method of a fitted estimator for each n_jobs value."""
    print(f"timing {label} ...", flush=True)
    times = {}
    for n in N_JOBS:
        fitted.set_params(n_jobs=n)
        times[n] = median_time(lambda: getattr(fitted, method)(X))
    return times


def fit_for_prediction(estimator):
    """Fit once with all jobs; prediction timings then change n_jobs only."""
    return estimator.set_params(n_jobs=max(N_JOBS))


# --- go/no-go checks --------------------------------------------------------


def is_parallel(times):
    """Clearly faster at 2 jobs than at 1, and never slower as n_jobs rises."""
    t = [times[n] for n in N_JOBS]
    return t[1] < CLEARLY_FASTER * t[0] and all(
        later <= NOISE * earlier for earlier, later in zip(t, t[1:])
    )


def stays_flat(times):
    """A fit that is mostly OOB scoring does not get faster as n_jobs rises."""
    base = times[N_JOBS[0]]
    return base > 0 and all(times[n] >= OOB_FLAT * base for n in N_JOBS)


def capped_at_two(times):
    """With 2 estimators, more than 2 jobs gives no further speed-up."""
    return all(times[n] >= CAP_FLAT * times[2] for n in N_JOBS if n > 2)


# --- modes ------------------------------------------------------------------


def calibrate(data):
    """Single runs at n_jobs=1, to pick data sizes before the full run."""
    X, y, X_pred = data["clf"]
    clf = BaggingClassifier(n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, n_jobs=1,
                            random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
    print(f"BaggingClassifier.fit            {run_once(lambda: clf.fit(X, y)):6.2f} s"
          "  (target 3-5 s)")
    print(f"BaggingClassifier.predict_proba  "
          f"{run_once(lambda: clf.predict_proba(X_pred)):6.2f} s  (target >= 1 s)")

    X, y, X_pred = data["reg"]
    reg = BaggingRegressor(n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, n_jobs=1,
                           random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
    print(f"BaggingRegressor.fit             {run_once(lambda: reg.fit(X, y)):6.2f} s"
          "  (target 3-5 s)")
    print(f"BaggingRegressor.predict         "
          f"{run_once(lambda: reg.predict(X_pred)):6.2f} s  (target >= 1 s)")

    X, y, X_pred = data["svc"]
    svc = fit_for_prediction(BaggingClassifier(
        SVC(), n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)).fit(X, y)
    svc.set_params(n_jobs=1)
    print(f"BaggingClassifier(SVC()).decision_function "
          f"{run_once(lambda: svc.decision_function(X_pred)):6.2f} s  (target >= 1 s)")

    for name, estimator_class, knn, (X, y) in [
        ("BaggingClassifier", BaggingClassifier, KNeighborsClassifier(), data["knn_clf"]),
        ("BaggingRegressor", BaggingRegressor, KNeighborsRegressor(), data["knn_reg"]),
    ]:
        est = estimator_class(knn, n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, oob_score=True,
                              n_jobs=1, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
        print(f"{name}(KNN).fit, oob_score=True "
              f"{run_once(lambda: est.fit(X, y)):6.2f} s  (target 3-5 s)")


def full_run(data):
    """Time every documented method and both controls; return table rows."""
    rows = []  # (label, times, check or None)

    X, y, X_pred = data["clf"]
    rows.append(("BaggingClassifier.fit",
                 time_fit("BaggingClassifier.fit", BaggingClassifier, X, y,
                          n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS),
                 is_parallel))
    clf = fit_for_prediction(BaggingClassifier(
        n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)).fit(X, y)
    for method in ["predict", "predict_proba", "predict_log_proba"]:
        label = f"BaggingClassifier.{method}"
        rows.append((label, time_method(label, clf, method, X_pred), is_parallel))

    X_svc, y_svc, X_svc_pred = data["svc"]
    svc = fit_for_prediction(BaggingClassifier(
        SVC(), n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)).fit(X_svc, y_svc)
    label = "BaggingClassifier(SVC()).decision_function"
    rows.append((label, time_method(label, svc, "decision_function", X_svc_pred),
                 is_parallel))

    Xr, yr, Xr_pred = data["reg"]
    rows.append(("BaggingRegressor.fit",
                 time_fit("BaggingRegressor.fit", BaggingRegressor, Xr, yr,
                          n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS),
                 is_parallel))
    reg = fit_for_prediction(BaggingRegressor(
        n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)).fit(Xr, yr)
    label = "BaggingRegressor.predict"
    rows.append((label, time_method(label, reg, "predict", Xr_pred), is_parallel))

    # Control 1: OOB scoring runs sequentially at the end of fit. KNN fits almost
    # instantly but is slow to predict, so this fit is mostly OOB scoring.
    for name, estimator_class, knn, (Xk, yk) in [
        ("BaggingClassifier", BaggingClassifier, KNeighborsClassifier(), data["knn_clf"]),
        ("BaggingRegressor", BaggingRegressor, KNeighborsRegressor(), data["knn_reg"]),
    ]:
        label = f"Control: {name}(KNN).fit, oob_score=True"
        rows.append((label,
                     time_fit(label, estimator_class, Xk, yk, estimator=knn,
                              n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, oob_score=True),
                     stays_flat))

    # Control 2: estimators are split into at most n_estimators groups
    label = "Control: BaggingClassifier.fit, n_estimators=2"
    rows.append((label, time_fit(label, BaggingClassifier, X, y, n_estimators=2),
                 capped_at_two))
    return rows


# --- report -----------------------------------------------------------------


def format_table(rows):
    first, last = N_JOBS[0], N_JOBS[-1]
    lines = [
        "| Timing (s) | " + " | ".join(f"n_jobs={n}" for n in N_JOBS)
        + f" | Speed-up {first} to {last} | Check |",
        "|---" * (len(N_JOBS) + 3) + "|",
    ]
    for label, times, check in rows:
        cells = " | ".join(f"{times[n]:.3f}" for n in N_JOBS)
        speedup = f"{times[first] / times[last]:.2f}x" if times[last] > 0 else "n/a"
        result = "" if check is None else ("pass" if check(times) else "FAIL")
        lines.append(f"| {label} | {cells} | {speedup} | {result} |")
    return "\n".join(lines)


def environment_report():
    buffer = io.StringIO()
    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buffer):
        sklearn.show_versions()
    return (f"Physical cores (joblib): {joblib.cpu_count(only_physical_cores=True)}\n"
            f"Logical cores (os): {os.cpu_count()}\n{buffer.getvalue()}")


def main():
    args = parse_args()
    data = make_data(args)
    if args.calibrate:
        calibrate(data)
        return

    rows = full_run(data)
    all_pass = all(check(times) for _, times, check in rows if check is not None)
    report = "\n\n".join([
        f"# Bagging n_jobs timing, {datetime.now():%Y-%m-%d %H:%M}",
        f"Settings: {vars(args)}, n_estimators={N_ESTIMATORS}, "
        f"n_features={N_FEATURES}, median of {N_REPEATS} runs after 1 warm-up, "
        "default joblib backend.",
        format_table(rows),
        f"Automatic checks: {'all pass (go)' if all_pass else 'some FAIL (review)'}",
        f"## Environment\n\n```\n{environment_report()}```",
    ])
    RESULTS_FILE.write_text(report + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    print("\n" + format_table(rows))
    print(f"\nAutomatic checks: {'all pass' if all_pass else 'some FAIL'}")
    print(f"Saved to {RESULTS_FILE}")


if __name__ == "__main__":  # required on Windows: joblib starts new processes
    main()
```

Run with: `python bagging_n_jobs_timing.py --clf-samples 2500 --reg-samples 3000 --predict-samples 60000 --svc-test 1000 --knn-samples 7500`

</details>

I wasn't sure whether the docstring should mention OOB scoring. With `oob_score=True`, the OOB step at the end of `fit` is a plain `for` loop over the estimators, so `n_jobs` doesn't speed it up. That's what the control row shows. I left it out to keep the docstring short and in line with RandomForest. Should I add a short note about it?

- OOB loop, classifier: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4358542a1bd39af2e7e1cbace8b9fed067473c5b/sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py#L896
- OOB loop, regressor: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4358542a1bd39af2e7e1cbace8b9fed067473c5b/sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py#L1454


#### Introduce yourself

I'm Nitin Mishra, a B.Tech student in Computer Science and AI at Tensor School of Computer Science and AI. I use scikit-learn in my ML trading projects and I'm interested in contributing to open source. I picked #14228 because it's a small docs change with a clear scope, and I could check it against the code and measure it on my own machine. This isn't my first PR, but feedback on how I could do better is very welcome. So are pointers on where to learn more and how to get to know other contributors.

I used Claude Code to trace where `n_jobs` is used in `_bagging.py`, to write the timing script, and to draft and edit this description. I checked the code paths and the timing results myself, chose the wording, and reviewed the docstring edit before committing it.

title: `CalibratedClassifierCV(method="sigmoid")` should always take the raw logits as inputs instead of the predicted probabilities
body: This is a defect [I first observed while reviewing the temperature scaling PR](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/31068#discussion_r2012459507): if the uncalibrated classifier only exposes a `decision_function` and no `predict_proba` (which is the case for SVMs for instance) our implementation of sigmoid calibration (aka Platt-scaling) is fine because the output values of `decision_function` are morally logits between -inf and +inf with 0 as the default decision threshold. But if the uncalibrated classifier already exposes a `predict_proba` method (e.g. `GaussianNB`), our current implementation takes the predicted probabilities as input of the parametrized sigmoid function. This is incorrect: we should the log of the probabilistic predictions (incremented by a small epsilon) to feed logits as inputs to the sigmoid function. I had started an unfinished WIP branch now turned into a draft PR (https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34313) to attempt to fix this problem and started to do empirical evaluation to assess the impact of this change in examples. Early results were very promising. However, it would now need work to be sync with main again after the merge of the temperature scaling PR and I got distracted and this was burried in my personal TODO list of WIP stuff to revive. Meanwhile, the following paper by @eugeneberta, @dholzmueller et al. was published, and it confirms that it is empirically much better to take the logits, in which case it is a very competitive calibration method (better than most other calibration methods on average on a large set of data & model pairs). CalArena: A Large-Scale Post-Hoc Calibration Benchmark https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30188 Side note: I suspect that OvR Platt-logits followed by post-hoc class-wise renormalization would also work very well in the multiclass setting, but this does not seem to have been explored in the above paper from a cursory glance. Do you confirm @eugeneberta, @dholzmueller?

title: FIX RadiusNeighborsRegressor silently returns a sentinel for empty neighborhoods with integer targets
body:
Reference Issues/PRs
--------------------
Fixes #12960.

What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
---------------------------------------------------

`RadiusNeighborsRegressor` builds the placeholder for samples with no neighbors
inside `radius` with:

```python
empty_obs = np.full_like(_y[0], np.nan)
```

`np.full_like` inherits the target dtype, and casting NaN into an integer target
is undefined. The result is a sentinel that is indistinguishable from a real
prediction:

```python
X = np.array([[0.0], [1.0], [2.0]])
est = RadiusNeighborsRegressor(radius=0.5).fit(X, np.array([0, 1, 2]))
est.predict([[100.0]])
# main: array([0])          <- 0 is a plausible prediction here
# this PR: array([nan]) + UserWarning
```

The reported value was `-9223372036854775808` in the original issue and is `0`
on numpy 2.x; either way it is platform-dependent garbage.

There is a second, worse consequence. The "no neighbors" warning is guarded by:

```python
if np.any(np.isnan(y_pred)):
```

`np.isnan` on an integer array is always `False`, so once the NaN had been cast
away the warning could never fire. Integer targets therefore failed silently in
both directions: wrong value *and* no warning. Float targets were unaffected,
which is why this went unnoticed.

Mixed batches were also affected, and this is the case most likely to reach a
user unnoticed:

```python
est = RadiusNeighborsRegressor(radius=0.6).fit(X, np.array([0, 1, 2]))
est.predict([[1.0], [100.0]])
# main:    array([1., 0.])    <- second entry is not a prediction
# this PR: array([ 1., nan]) + UserWarning
```

The fix promotes the placeholder to a float dtype so NaN is representable:

```python
empty_obs = np.full_like(
    _y[0], np.nan, dtype=np.promote_types(_y.dtype, np.float16)
)
```

`np.promote_types(dtype, np.float16)` reproduces the dtype `np.mean` already
returns for the non-empty rows (`int32/int64 -> float64`, `float32 -> float32`,
`float64 -> float64`), so predictions are unchanged wherever neighbors exist and
`float32` targets keep their precision rather than being widened.

Any other comments?
-------------------

**Tests.** Two non-regression tests, ten parametrised cases: empty
neighborhoods across `int32/int64/float32/float64` and both weightings, and a
partially-empty batch. Each asserts NaN, a floating result dtype, and that the
`UserWarning` actually fires. Against `main` five of the ten fail (every integer
case); all ten pass with this change.

**Validation caveat, stated plainly.** I could not build scikit-learn from source
on this machine; the C++ toolchain fails on the macOS SDK headers, unrelated to
this change. I validated by applying the patched `_regression.py` over an
installed 1.8.0 and running `sklearn.neighbors.tests.test_neighbors`:

```
pristine 1.8.0, its own tests                     585 passed, 436 skipped
patched _regression.py, its own tests             585 passed, 436 skipped
```

identical, so no regression in the released test suite. Running `main`'s test
file against installed 1.8.0 produces 10 pre-existing failures purely from the
version skew (confirmed with none of my changes applied), and the same 10 with
this change plus my 10 new tests passing. CI here is authoritative over my local
numbers.

One incidental effect: the fix removes roughly 185 spurious
`RuntimeWarning: invalid value encountered in cast` warnings from that test run.

**One design question for the reviewer.** I kept the existing contract of
NaN-plus-`UserWarning` rather than raising, since that is what float targets have
always done and changing it would be a behaviour break for them. Integer targets
now simply behave like float ones. If the preference is to raise on empty
neighborhoods, that is a different and larger change and I am happy to take it
instead.

I used AI assistance for:
- Code generation (fixing the bug)
- Test/benchmark generation
- Drafting this PR description

Per the Automated Contributions Policy, the change was reviewed, run and verified before
submission rather than submitted unread.

title: PRF: Over-subscription in pairwise_distances with `backend="threading"` + BLAS-pthreads

labels.name: Parallelism and scalability
labels.description: All things related to efficient handling of cores via thread-based or process-based parallelism.

body:
> 🚨 This is a complex issue that already has experts working on it. Please don't start work on this without first coordinating with them.

`sklearn.metrics.pairwise_distances` accepts a `n_jobs` parameters and uses `joblib.Parallel(backend="threading", n_jobs=n_jobs)` under-the-hood. But this parallelization happens on top on openBLAS parallelism, and can lead to what looks like over-subscription.

(but maybe it's not over-subscription, and something else, like cost of repeated small parallelized blas calls, etc. I haven't investigated) 

Results from a small benchmark script shows that limiting blas to 1 thread helps scaling as `n_jobs` grows (and usually achieves best performance compared to n_jobs=1 with blas parallelism enabled):

``` 
--- n_samples=2000  n_features=200 ---
  n_jobs=  1 | pin-blas=0:      33ms

title: FIX Nystroem with precomputed kernel and n_components < n_samples
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Fixes #29353

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

When kernel="precomputed", Nystroem.fit only subsampled the rows of the
kernel matrix. That left a non-square basis kernel of shape
(n_components, n_samples), so pairwise_kernels raised a ValueError and you
could never set n_components smaller than n_samples with a precomputed
kernel.

The fix takes the square submatrix indexed by basis_inds on both axes for the
basis kernel, and slices the basis columns in transform. A sparse CSR
precomputed kernel is densified with .toarray() before the svd and the
normalization matmul, because np.asarray does not densify scipy sparse
matrices.

I also kept the validation that used to come for free through
pairwise_kernels: gamma, coef0 and degree are still rejected for a
precomputed kernel, and the precomputed fit kernel must be square. A
non-square precomputed kernel now raises a clear error message.

Two new non-regression tests cover this. One checks that fit_transform with a
precomputed RBF kernel and n_components < n_samples matches passing the data
directly with kernel="rbf", for both dense and CSR input. The other checks
the clear error on a non-square precomputed kernel.

I reviewed, built, and tested all of these changes myself, I understand them,

body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Closes #26369.

This revives the fix from the stale #26480 (no maintainer review since Jan 2024), but keeps the change minimal: it does **not** add the extra `tol`-sign validation that PR proposed, since the `tol` docstring already documents that `tol` may be negative for backward selection.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

For `SequentialFeatureSelector` with `direction="backward"` and `n_features_to_select="auto"`, `old_score` was initialized to `-np.inf`, exactly as for forward selection. The auto-selection stopping criterion is:

```python
if is_auto_select and ((new_score - old_score) < self.tol):
    break
```

On the first backward iteration this is `(new_score - (-inf)) < tol` → `inf < tol` → always `False`, so the loop never stops on the first step and **at least one feature is always removed**, even when removing any feature decreases the score. (As noted by `@betatim` in the issue, this was the root cause.)

The fix initializes `old_score`, for backward auto-selection only, to the cross-validation score obtained with **all** features — the correct reference point for deciding whether the first removal is worthwhile. Forward selection keeps the `-np.inf` initialization (its reference is "no features yet"). The extra `cross_val_score` call is only performed in the backward auto-select case, so other code paths are unaffected.

Reproducer from the issue (all features informative, so removing any hurts):

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
from sklearn.feature_selection import SequentialFeatureSelector
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X, y = make_regression(n_samples=100, n_features=3, n_informative=3, noise=0, random_state=0)
sfs = SequentialFeatureSelector(
    LinearRegression(), n_features_to_select="auto", tol=0, direction="backward", cv=2
).fit(X, y)
print(sfs.get_support())   # before: one feature dropped; after: [ True  True  True ]
```

#### Any other comments?

- Added a non-regression test (`test_backward_auto_keeps_all_features_when_removal_hurts`).
- Updated `test_n_features_to_select_auto`: the backward case previously relied on the buggy behavior (positive `tol` + all-informative data forced a removal). It now uses a negative `tol` for backward (as the docstring sanctions) and data with uninformative features, so backward selection correctly drops only the uninformative ones.
- Full `test_sequential.py` suite passes locally (75 passed).

title: Clarify parameter/hyperparameter terminology in the cross-validation workflow diagram
body:
### Introduce yourself

I teach machine learning engineering to people who are new to machine learning.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

I use `GridSearchCV` to help learners understand grid search, model selection, and good practice. I think it is a fantastic teaching tool, and the user guide is excellent.

I've taught this section several times and have repeatedly needed to explain why the diagram says "parameters" when we are discussing hyperparameters. This is a recurring point of confusion in my teaching, which prompted this issue.

The overall workflow diagram in the cross-validation user guide uses the labels **"Parameters"** and **"Best parameters"**.

User guide:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html

Direct link to the diagram:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/_images/grid_search_workflow.png

My learners are meeting the terms "parameter" and "hyperparameter" for the first time. They are still learning the difference between settings we specify or search over, such as a decision tree's maximum depth, and values the model learns during fitting.

When I explain grid search, I describe it as comparing hyperparameter settings. The diagram calls these "Parameters" and "Best parameters". I then have to explain why the same settings are being called by two different names, while learners are still trying to understand what those names mean.

I understand that scikit-learn uses "parameters" for estimator constructor settings. The glossary explains this convention:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/glossary.html#term-parameter

The cross-validation guide also uses the word "hyperparameters". A short explanation at the diagram would help beginners connect the two terms.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Could a short note be added beside or below the diagram to explain how "parameters" relates to "hyperparameters"? For example:

> Here, "parameters" means configurable estimator settings. These can include machine-learning hyperparameters, such as a decision tree's `max_depth`, as well as other configuration choices, such as which estimator or pipeline step to use. They are different from values learned by the model during fitting.

The note could link to the glossary:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/glossary.html#term-parameter

The diagram could keep its existing labels. The note would help beginners understand why settings such as `max_depth` may be called "hyperparameters" in machine-learning terminology while scikit-learn uses the broader term "parameters".

title: DOC: clarify that recursion method computes conditional partial dependence
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs
Fixes #27441 (documentation aspect).

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

Issue #27441 reports that `partial_dependence()` gives different results for `method='recursion'` vs `method='brute'` on tree-based estimators when features are correlated, and asks for the documentation to clarify the distinction rather than leaving it implicit.

The existing `pdp_method_differences` note says the methods "might differ" but does not explain the semantic root cause. This PR makes the distinction explicit:

1. **`doc/modules/partial_dependence.rst`** — extends the note to state that `'brute'` computes the **interventional** PDP `E[f(x_S, X_C) | do(X_S = x_S)]` (the quantity typically intended), while `'recursion'` (tree-based only) computes the **conditional** PDP `E[f(x_S, X_C) | X_S = x_S]`, which reflects the training data's correlation structure. Explicitly states the two are not equivalent for tree-based estimators when features are correlated.

2. **`sklearn/inspection/_partial_dependence.py`** — adds a one-line pointer in the `'brute'` bullet of the `method` parameter docstring so the distinction is visible at the API surface, not only in the narrative docs.

No code behavior is changed. This is a pure documentation clarification that directly addresses what the issue asks for ("it should be communicated clearly in the documentation that (i) the two methods are not equivalent for tree based algorithms, and (ii) that method = 'recursion' actually computes the conditional ... instead of the ... interventional ...").

title: FIX Reference-count BLAS thread limit in pairwise distance reductions
body:
<!--
Thanks for contributing a pull request! Please ensure you have taken a look at
the contribution guidelines: https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/index.html
-->

#### Reference Issues/PRs
Fixes #31884

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
When calling `ArgKmin64.compute()` or `RadiusNeighbors64.compute()` concurrently across threads (e.g. using `joblib.Parallel(backend="threading")`), numerical corruption occurs in environments running OpenBLAS compiled with the OpenMP threading layer.

The root cause is overlapping `threadpoolctl` context manager lifecycles: `threadpoolctl` changes process-global C state (`openblas_set_num_threads`). When Thread A exits its `compute()` block, it prematurely restores the thread limit back to default (e.g. 12) while concurrent threads are still running `_gemm` operations, corrupting OpenBLAS's non-reentrant static packing buffers.

This PR introduces `_RefcountedBLASLimit` in `sklearn.utils.parallel`. It reference-counts concurrent entries across threads so the BLAS thread limit stays pinned to 1 as long as any reduction is active, and only restores the original thread count once the last concurrent thread exits.

#### Any other comments?
- Added unit tests for `_RefcountedBLASLimit` in `test_parallel.py`.
- Added a multithreaded regression test in `test_pairwise_distances_reduction.py`.
- Included a towncrier news entry.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

StandardScaler.fit() silently returns a scale of 1.0 (instead of erroring or
warning) when a feature has zero or near-zero variance — e.g. a single-sample
fit, or a constant column. This is implemented via the internal
_handle_zeros_in_scale helper, but the behavior is not mentioned in the
public StandardScaler docstring or the User Guide.

Minimal reproduction:

​```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[1, 2, 3]])  # single sample — zero variance
scaler = StandardScaler()
print(scaler.fit_transform(X))
# Output: [[0., 0., 0.]] — no warning, no error raised

unusual happened.

Adding a note to the StandardScaler docstring (and the corresponding section of the User Guide at doc/modules/preprocessing.rst) explaining that when a feature has zero or near-zero variance, its scale_ is set to 1.0 rather than raising an error or leaving a zero — so the transformed output for that feature will be 0. rather than NaN or inf. title: RFC Always store fitted attributes as Numpy
body:

> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

This is an issue related to #34152 but is also a standalone issue.

While thinking about #34152 and working on #34324 I thought that it might be a good idea if the fitted attributes of an estimator were always Numpy arrays. The current plan is to store fitted attributes in the namespace/device of `X`.

Reasons to do this:
1. users most often use fitted attributes for inspection/debugging/plotting. Having them in a consistent array namespace makes this easy to do. If the namespace is input dependent then you have to change your debugging/plotting code. Say you run the same script on a machine with a CUDA GPU and on your laptop with no GPU. While it is not difficult to use write code that uses `move_to()` to conditionally bring the attributes to Numpy for plotting, it is tedious.
2. Today attributes are Numpy, by keeping them Numpy we remove one source of bugs/differences. Enabling array API by default would not change this
3. Part of #34324 that is not great/tricky is dealing with estimators that sometimes support array API. For example for some hyper-parameter values array API is supported and for some not. The tricky question: What should the type of the fitted attributes be?
4. You can `fit` with one array namespace/device and `predict` with a different one without any conversion
5. An estimator fitted with pytorch/CUDA can be unpickled on a machine without CUDA and even without pytorch

Something to check is how much overhead/performance loss we get in `predict` and other inference methods if we have to convert the fitted attributes relevant for predicting from Numpy to the array namespace of the input each time. Though I suspect that conversion is fast. It might add appreciable overhead if you are predicting on very few samples, but the absolute time will be short in those cases (and you could just use the CPU?). We would need to introduce a way to make it easy to convert fitted attributes to Numpy in each estimator to avoid lots of boilerplate. What are other reasons to not do this?

What do others think?

title: FIX Prevent segfault in TSNE with PCA init on constant data
body:
#### Reference Issue
Fixes #28368 (ref: #32788 which is a duplicate issue)

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
This PR fixes a bug where `TSNE` with `init='pca'` produces `NaN` values (leading to potential segmentation faults in the C++ extension) when the input data has zero variance (constant values).

**The Issue:**
In `_t_sne.py`, the PCA initialization step attempts to normalize the first principal component by dividing by its standard deviation: `X_embedded / np.std(...)`. When the input data is constant, the standard deviation is `0.0`, resulting in `NaN` propagation.

**The Fix:**
I added a safe-guard check for the standard deviation.
- If `std < 1e-12` (effectively zero), the division is skipped, and the embedding is only scaled by the default factor (`1e-4`).
- Otherwise, the standard normalization logic is applied.

**Verification:**
Added a regression test `test_tsne_pca_init_constant_data` in `sklearn/manifold/tests/test_t_sne.py` which asserts that fitting on a constant matrix (`np.ones`) produces finite values and does not crash.

#### Other comments
The fix uses a tolerance check (`< 1e-12`) rather than strict equality (`== 0`) to handle floating-point nuances, ensuring robustness for near-constant data.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

I'd love to push the inspection module further by adding Accumulated local effects (ALE) from Apley 2020. A great description can be found in Christoph's online book https://christophm.github.io/interpretable-ml-book/ale.html

ALE fix the problem of partial dependence that they force the model to be evaluated on impossible or rare feature combinations. ALE are defined for numeric features that can be binned. From both bin edges, the slope of the partial dependence is calculated locally, i.e., only using observations in the bin. The slopes from all bins are cumsummed and vertically centered to the average response or prediction.

### Reference

Apley, Daniel W., and Jingyu Zhu. 2020. Visualizing the Effects of Predictor Variables in Black Box Supervised Learning Models. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B: Statistical Methodology, 82 (4): 1059–1086. doi:10.1111/rssb.12377.

### Describe your proposed solution

Pseudo code to calculate ALE for one feature:

``` py
pd_slopes = np.zeros_like(bins)

for i, bin in enumerate(bins):
  X_bin = pick n_per_bin = 200 rows from data in bin
  if X_bin is empty:
    next
  pd = partial_dependence_brute(model, X_bin, grid = [lower bin edge, upper bin edge], sample_weights)
  pd_slopes[i] = pd[1] - pd[0]

return np.cumsum(pd_slopes)
